questions.question: What are the two distinct ideas the author says get lumped together under the label "distributed representations"?
questions.referenceAnswer: Composition, where independent features (like color and shape) combine to represent objects, and superposition, where more features are packed into fewer neurons than there are dimensions, relying on sparsity and a non-linearity to retrieve them. The author argues these are different strategies with different properties, not points on one spectrum.

questions.question: What is the main cost of the "dense" maximal superposition code that can represent all colored shapes with only four neurons?
questions.referenceAnswer: You lose the ability to linearly select most individual colors or shapes (or sets of them) with a probe, and you generally can't represent objects "between" features, like a purple square with rounded corners.

questions.question: In the pure "local code" example, where every neuron represents one specific (shape, color) pair, what surprising advantage does this seemingly wasteful scheme have?
questions.referenceAnswer: Despite using a neuron for every combination, it is extremely flexible: it can represent arbitrary sets of stimuli at once, and a future layer can linearly select almost any combination of features (e.g. firing for black circles and white triangles but not black triangles or white circles), which other codes cannot do.

questions.question: Why does the compositional code need far fewer neurons than the local code, according to the article?
questions.referenceAnswer: Because independent features can compose together, n feature neurons (like separate color and shape neurons) can represent an exponential number of combinations, roughly exp(n), rather than needing a separate neuron for every possible combination as the local code does.

questions.question: What kind of generalization benefit does the compositional ("semi-local") code offer that the article calls "non-local generalization"?
questions.referenceAnswer: Because objects are represented by combining independent features like color and shape, learning something about one combination (e.g. green circles) can transfer to another combination sharing a feature (e.g. green squares), even without direct data on it.

questions.question: Why does the dense/maximal superposition code have to abandon the independent color and shape features used by the compositional code?
questions.referenceAnswer: The article explains that maximal superposition is only possible if there isn't composition, so the dense code has to go back to using non-composing (color, shape) combination features, like the local code, rather than independently composing color and shape features.

questions.question: Why does the author caution against concluding, just because a linear probe can detect "red" in the local code example, that the code actually has a "red" feature?
questions.referenceAnswer: The local code represents whole (color, shape) pairs, not independent color and shape features, so even though a probe can pick out the direction corresponding to redness across the red-associated neurons, it doesn't mean the underlying representation is organized around a distinct "red" feature the way a compositional code would be.

questions.question: In Thorpe's "semi-distributed" code, how does the author suggest we should think about which neuron groupings correspond to which features?
questions.referenceAnswer: Even though individual neurons are polysemantic (each responds to a few different things), the author suggests thinking of linear combinations of neurons, i.e. directions, as corresponding to features - for example, one pair of neurons summing to represent "Green" and another pair summing to represent "Square."

questions.question: Using the article's argument about "volume," why can't a representation have both full composition and full superposition of the same features at once?
questions.referenceAnswer: With m bits/neurons there is an exponential amount of representational volume, exp(m). Storing n features that can arbitrarily compose requires exp(n) volume, which uses up essentially all of it, leaving no room to additionally cram in far more items via superposition; superposition only works when there's no composition, letting exp(m) unrelated items be packed in instead.

questions.question: How can composition and superposition coexist in the same representation, according to the article's discussion of sparsity?
questions.referenceAnswer: When features are sparse, meaning most combinations of them are rare or mutually exclusive rather than dense, the compositional space has "holes" or low-probability regions of unused volume, and these unused regions can be exploited to store additional features in superposition alongside the composing ones.
